content: Pasteurization is a process that involves heating liquids to eliminate viruses and harmful microorganisms, including bacteria, protozoa, molds, and yeasts. This method is named after its inventor, Louis Pasteur, a French chemist and microbiologist. The first successful pasteurization test was conducted by Pasteur and Claude Bernard on April 20, 1862. Unlike sterilization, pasteurization does not aim to eradicate all microorganisms in food. Instead, it seeks to achieve a logarithmic reduction in the number of viable organisms, reducing their population to levels unlikely to cause disease, provided the product is refrigerated and consumed before its expiration date. Sterilization on a commercial scale is uncommon due to its negative impact on the taste and quality of food products. Pasteurization typically employs temperatures below the boiling point. For example, heating milk above its boiling point can cause casein micelles to irreversibly aggregate, leading to curdling. There are two primary pasteurization methods in use today: High Temperature/Short Time (HTST) and Extended Shelf Life (ESL) treatment. Ultra-High Temperature (UHT), also known as Ultra-Heat Treated, is another method used for milk processing. HTST involves heating milk to 72°C (161°F) for 15–20 seconds, while UHT processing heats milk to 138°C (250°F) for a fraction of a second. ESL milk undergoes microbial filtration and is treated at lower temperatures than HTST. Milk labeled simply as pasteurized is usually treated with the HTST method, whereas milk labeled ultra-pasteurized or UHT is processed using the UHT method. National food safety agencies, such as the USDA in the United States and the Food Standards Agency in the United Kingdom, regulate and standardize pasteurization methods. These agencies require milk to be HTST pasteurized to qualify for the pasteurized label. Different dairy products have varying pasteurization standards based on their fat content and intended use. For instance, the standards for cream differ from those for fluid milk, and cheese pasteurization standards are designed to preserve the phosphatase enzyme, which aids in the cheese-making process. Pasteurization is effective in reducing viable microorganisms in milk by a factor of 10,000 (a 4-log reduction). This level of reduction is sufficient to destroy nearly all yeasts, molds, and common spoilage bacteria, as well as heat-resistant pathogenic organisms such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis (which causes tuberculosis) and Coxiella burnetii (which causes Q fever). HTST pasteurization processes must ensure even heating of the milk, with no portion subjected to shorter times or lower temperatures. A newer method, known as flash pasteurization, involves exposing products to higher temperatures for shorter durations. This technique is claimed to better preserve the color and taste of certain products. Additionally, food irradiation is sometimes referred to as electronic pasteurization, as it uses radiation to kill bacteria in food. Pasteurization is commonly associated with milk, a practice first proposed by Franz von Soxhlet in 1886. HTST-pasteurized milk typically has a refrigerated shelf life of two to three weeks, while ultra-pasteurized milk can last two to three months when refrigerated. When UHT treatment is combined with sterile handling and aseptic packaging, milk can be stored unrefrigerated for three to four months. Alternative pasteurization methods include batch pasteurization, which involves heating large quantities of milk to 68°C (145°F) for 30 minutes, followed by rapid cooling to about 4°C (39°F). Another technique, known as Higher-Heat/Shorter Time (HHST), falls between HTST and UHT in terms of time and temperature. Pasteurization causes some irreversible and some temporary denaturation of milk proteins. In 2001, the USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service considered implementing new rules requiring double pasteurization, which would involve holding milk at 72°C (161°F) for two separate 15-second periods instead of one 30-second period. However, in most jurisdictions, milk treated by double pasteurization might not be considered pasteurized, depending on the temperature and duration of the heat treatment. Heat treatment at lower temperatures or for shorter times may also be performed, but such milk might be labeled as raw milk or unpasteurized milk, even though a significant number of pathogens are destroyed during the process. Pasteurization can prevent diseases such as tuberculosis, diphtheria, polio, salmonella, strep throat, scarlet fever, and typhoid fever. In regions like Africa and South Asia, it is common to boil milk to sterilize it after harvesting. This intense heating significantly alters the flavor of milk, which is often preferred by local populations. Recent advancements in diagnostic techniques, such as real-time PCR and improved culture methods, have enabled researchers to detect pathogens in pasteurized milk, raising questions about whether current pasteurization standards are adequate.
